disclaimer: Only findings confirmed word for word at the source get in. Where two serious studies disagree, we publish both and explain why they disagree — we do not pick the one that flatters the argument.
verdict[0].finding: The revenue-sharing system cannot equalise the states' fiscal capacity, nor reduce the inequality between them — which is the job the Constitution gives it.
verdict[1].finding: Brazil's intergovernmental transfers are not effective at reducing fiscal inequality between states: according to the study, simulations show middle-income states receiving more transfers than the poorest ones (paraphrase).
counterpoint.title: Counting only transfers gives one picture. Counting all spending gives another.
counterpoint.finding: A study by FGV IBRE reaches a conclusion that cuts against the simple story that the south and southeast 'carry the country on their backs'. Measuring total federal spending in each state — not just transfers — Rio de Janeiro gets back more than it contributes (10.4% of federal spending against 9.4% of revenue), and Minas Gerais and Espírito Santo weigh more in population than in revenue. The south and southeast account for 71% of federal revenue with 57% of the population.
originCaveat.finding: And there is a distortion that poisons any 'who pays' map: federal revenue is recorded at the company's tax domicile, not where the activity happened. The clearest case is the Federal District, which collected R$ 158 billion in federal taxes in 2022 — more than Minas Gerais (R$ 141 billion), a state with almost seven times as many people. It is not Brasília's economy that produces this: it is the address of the head office. By the same mechanism, São Paulo accounts for 43.4% of all personal income tax in the country. Anyone publishing a 'who supports whom' map without that caveat is manufacturing a fight between states with a number that does not mean what it appears to.
sanitationExtremes.metric: % of urban households connected to the sewage network
piauiCase.title: The state that climbed most in HDI still has no sewage
piauiCase.finding: Piauí is one of the states most dependent on transfers in the country, and this is the number the government shows: its HDI went from 0.480 in 2000 to 0.710 in 2020, the biggest rise in Brazil over the period. In that same Piauí, only 23.3% of urban households have a sewage connection — close to the worst rate in the country. Twenty years of money arriving, and the basics never did.
returnRatio.narrowRuler.explain: It counts only what the union transfers to state and city governments — the FPE, FPM and similar funds. It is the ruler behind most headlines.
returnRatio.confirmation.finding: A second independent calculation, by Poder360 using 2021 data, arrived at the same shape: the south, the southeast and — for the first time since the series began in 2014 — the whole centre-west paid more than they received. Every state in the northeast received more than it paid; in the north, the only exception was Amazonas.
returnRatio.broadRuler.explain: It also counts state pensions, federal civil servants' pay and pensions, federal universities and health units. It is federal money landing in the state through any door — and the result is almost a different country.

returnRatio.keyInsight.title: The number that explains the whole quarrel
returnRatio.keyInsight.finding: São Paulo receives 9% of the R$ 505 billion the union transfers directly to states and cities — and receives 28% of the R$ 734 billion it spends on pension benefits. The money does come back; it comes back as a pension, not as revenue sharing. Count only transfers and you see a plundered state; count the whole spend and you see a different picture. Both numbers are true — what changes is what each one decided to call a "return".
returnRatio.officialGap.finding: A curiosity that says a great deal: both halves of this calculation are public and official — the tax authority publishes how much each state collects, and the Treasury and the transparency portal publish how much each state receives. No government body puts the two together. The ones doing the division are the press and academia.
howItWorks[0].label: is the sharing rule of the State Participation Fund in the ORIGINAL wording of Complementary Law 62/1989: 85% of the pot to the north, northeast and centre-west; 15% to the south and southeast. It applied until 31 December 2015. Complementary Law 143/2013 did not keep that text — it replaced it with calculated coefficients, which the Supreme Court declared unconstitutional in 2023 (ADI 5069), modulating the effects and extending the provisional rule because Congress never legislated. The regional design is the same; what changed is how each state’s number is reached.
howItWorks[1].label: In 2022, the states sent R$ 2.218 trillion in federal taxes and R$ 607.8 billion came back as transfers to states and municipalities. Mind the ruler: transfers are not the whole return — state pensions, federal civil servants' pay, federal universities and health-system funding are also federal money landing in the state, and they are not in this calculation.
